talks.title: The Cybersecurity Days of Thunder: Driving Faster w/Good Brakes
talks.teaser: Argues that security leaders must protect their teams, communities, careers and health to keep moving fast.
talks.summary:
This RVAsec 2021 keynote looks at the non-technical questions security leaders are asking after nearly two years of the pandemic. The speaker describes a run of pressures: disrupted remote work, hard-to-fill roles, an expected wave of resignations, and a flood of conflicting information. The framing is that overwhelm, more than any particular attack technique, is now the main problem to manage.

The talk is organized around five areas to look after. For teams, the advice is to check in regularly, listen, recognize routine work, allow flexibility, offer stretch opportunities, and benchmark pay, since recruiting replacements is costly. For the community, colleagues, career and health, it recommends volunteering for nonprofits, mentoring and teaching, sharing lessons learned through local peer groups, building virtual connections, finding mentors, and keeping skills current. A personal account of a health scare after many months of travel illustrates why self-care matters for leaders.

The takeaway is that meeting basic human needs and protecting your own wellbeing come before the technical work, and that leaders who look after themselves are better placed to look after others.

talks.title: Why I love Purple Teams, even though they don't exist
talks.teaser: Questions whether purple teams are a real separate team and argues for better red and blue communication instead.
talks.summary:
Anthony Switzer opens by asking whether purple teaming is an actual team at all. He notes that the term is loosely defined in the industry and that almost no one in the room identifies as working on one. He traces his own path through certifications and penetration testing, arguing that security work should help businesses prevent and fix problems, not only break things.

The middle of the talk looks at why red and blue teams often compete rather than cooperate. Switzer describes the common siloed organization, where technical staff rarely communicate across groups, and contrasts it with a matrix structure that uses a cross-functional project to connect them. He suggests that blue defenders should build enough offensive knowledge to understand attacker motives and likely next steps. He frames purple teaming as largely a communication and education problem, and argues that many organizations may not need a new team at all.

He closes by encouraging attendees to look outside security for solutions other industries have already used, to learn business language, and to consider moving from technical roles toward the business side. In the question period, he suggested that blue teamers can gain red-team knowledge through training rather than through a separate purple team.

talks.title: Bake Security into your Infrastructure-as-Code
talks.teaser: Shows how to build security checks into infrastructure-as-code pipelines using misconfiguration scanners and secrets handling.
talks.summary:
The talk targets teams running workloads in public cloud, hybrid or on-prem environments, not only those already using infrastructure as code. It opens with the case for the approach: provisioning is faster than manual setup, the same code can reproduce production in dev and test, changes are tracked in source control for auditing, and environments can be rebuilt in another region after an attack. It also makes the point that infrastructure code is not secure just because it is code, so the resulting environment has to be verified.

The middle section compares major cloud providers and infrastructure-as-code tools such as Terraform, CloudFormation and Chef. It explains the three kinds of state involved: what is actually deployed, what the code describes, and what the tool records in its state file. The speaker then walks through a CI/CD pipeline with security stages and surveys open-source scanners that catch misconfigurations, using a short GitLab pipeline job to show how little configuration a scan stage needs.

For secrets and governance, the talk introduces the acronym BRUCE: build security gates into the pipeline, remove plaintext passwords, use a secrets server, check commit history for sensitive data, and encrypt secrets. It warns against making manual security fixes outside the code, since that causes drift between the deployed and described states. The closing advice is to practise with free cloud tiers and a tool like Jenkins, avoid assuming infrastructure code is secure, and automate checks wherever possible.

talks.title: Zero Trust: The Good Parts
talks.teaser: Walks through how one company moved its workforce from VPN perimeter access to zero trust identity-aware access.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a three-year effort at Cloudflare to replace VPN-based perimeter access with zero trust identity and access management across a workforce of a few thousand people. It starts from the premise that access should never depend on network position or IP address, and explains why cloud services, DevOps and containers made the old model unworkable.

The rollout began with web applications. The team built an identity-aware proxy that checked identity provider logins and issued session cookies, then placed a small set of internal tools behind it to show value before protecting everything. Hardware security keys replaced weaker second factors, with keys mailed to staff and enforcement phased in, first on a handful of sensitive applications and later across the board. Access control moved from subnet-based rules tracked in spreadsheets to identity provider groups. For SSH and other raw TCP services, the team tunneled TCP over an HTTP/2 connection and tested short-lived SSH certificates.

The later sections turned to device identity. Corporate machines received WireGuard clients tied to device serial numbers, and client certificates for mutual TLS were being phased in, with endpoint posture checks delegated to specialist vendors. Experimental work included an SSH client compiled to WebAssembly in the browser and a remote browser running on the edge. The main takeaways are to enforce a phishing-resistant second factor, solve both HTTP and non-HTTP access, and build strong device identity.

talks.title: Infrastructure as Code: Theory and Concepts
talks.teaser: Explains infrastructure as code concepts, object-oriented patterns, and the path from scripts to CI/CD and DevOps practice.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for managing infrastructure through code instead of manual configuration. The presenter lists the practical gains: faster and repeatable deployments, a version-controlled record of changes that doubles as documentation, and simpler rollback. Infrastructure is defined broadly, covering network devices, servers, load balancers and other connected systems that can be managed programmatically.

The middle section connects software design to infrastructure work. Object-oriented ideas such as code reuse, loose coupling and single responsibility are applied to deployment scripts, with a class-based VPC example compared against a procedural approach. Factory and builder patterns are presented as ways to move from large monolithic templates toward modular environments. Operations are mapped to create, read, update, delete and upsert, which then become API calls. Postman and vendor SDKs are shown as ways to generate usable code, and configuration management and cloud-native template tools are surveyed.

The closing part connects these practices to CI/CD and DevOps. Pipelines add build, test and gated delivery stages, and version history gives auditors a record of changes, including when and where they were applied. The presenter argues that DevOps is mainly about organizational process and collaboration rather than tools, and recommends starting with one small target, such as a single firewall, before expanding. Audience questions covered winning over reluctant teams and applying these ideas where duties are segregated.

talks.title: 5.4 Million Vulnerabilities and Counting...
talks.teaser: Presents a six-domain framework for building an enterprise vulnerability management program from a large shipbuilder's experience.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads a four-person vulnerability management team at a large manufacturer with roughly 70,000 to 80,000 devices, explains how the program began in 2017 with known problems: growing regulatory and contractual pressure, weak scanning, patching that lost out to operational work, and unclear ownership. Vulnerability counts climbed from about 300,000 to over a million as workstations were added to scanning, and an overdue backlog grew each month.

The team restructured in 2019, drove the overdue backlog down sharply, and built a shared knowledge base so that many administrators stopped duplicating research. Much of patching moved to automated tooling and remediation was centralized. From this experience the speaker proposed a six-domain framework: asset management, administrative controls, detection, prioritization and mitigation, remediation, and metrics reporting. Asset management comes first, combining static and dynamic inventories and recording both device owners and software owners. Detection should run at least as often as the patch SLA requires, and patch installation has to be verified rather than assumed.

The talk also covered treating out-of-band emergency patches as incident response, tailoring metrics to senior management, middle management and the people doing the patching, and formally accepting residual risk. The speaker reported remediation rates around 98 percent over several years. The takeaway for practitioners is to establish inventory, ownership and verification before chasing raw vulnerability counts, and to size the program to the organization's actual risk exposure.

talks.title: Introduction to inner-loop security. Shifting left, but better.
talks.teaser: Argues that application security tooling should fit the developer's local inner loop to shift left effectively.
talks.summary:
Josh Wallace opens by questioning the familiar shift-left pitch that many application security programs are built around. He traces the term back to a 2001 quality assurance article, arguing its original idea was testing throughout development rather than pushing security scanners onto developers. He then explains how the meaning drifted and critiques common tooling: static analysis, dynamic analysis, software composition analysis and manual penetration testing. Each is assessed for slow feedback, false positives, configuration effort and the time it takes from a developer's day. Security champion programs and developer performance reviews also come in for criticism.

The middle of the talk introduces the inner loop, the cycle from writing code through building, testing and committing locally, before a pull request moves work into the outer loop of CI/CD. Wallace frames slow, noisy steps as tax and waste, and proposes testing for agreed security controls rather than individual vulnerabilities. Those controls can be expressed as fast, automated checks, which he calls security as code, and he suggests that some scanners could then run less often in the pipeline.

He closes by arguing that security activity belongs in the inner loop where feedback is quick and accurate, while the outer loop keeps the checks that must run there. The takeaway for practitioners is to measure the developer impact of each control, reduce waste, and avoid shifting left simply for its own sake.

talks.title: Network Assessments: Cybersecurity, quackery and fraud
talks.teaser: Examines how network assessments get misused as quick fixes and outlines governance basics small businesses can follow instead.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a skeptical look at network assessments, a term the speaker argues has become vague, and at a vendor marketing claim that managed service providers close seven in ten new deals with them. Karl Jankowski, speaking from a managed service provider's perspective, traces the history of configuration checking tools and then tests the claim by searching for images, reviewing a product's user guide and running its scanner in a lab. He describes the resulting report as alarming by design, relying on red flags and urgency to push buyers toward a fast purchase.

The middle of the talk reframes the work as cybersecurity evaluation built on a chosen framework. He covers plain-language policies, a written incident response plan, and a short list of controls such as multi-factor authentication, periodic access and software reviews, and a 3-2-1 backup rule. He suggests simple documentation, a relational database for tracking assets and vendors, and free tools such as CSET. He also notes that vulnerability scans and CVE lists only matter once the business knows what it is trying to protect.

He closes by urging small companies to decide what level of security they can sustain, break the problem into small steps, and stay curious and methodical. The practical takeaway is that a scan is useful only after the organization understands its own risks and has committed to a process.

talks.title: What’s Next In The Fight Against Ransomware
talks.teaser: Traces how ransomware gangs operate and how policy and layered defenses could change the fight against them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of the problem. Ransomware has become more common and more profitable, with attackers adding extra extortion steps such as threatening to leak stolen data or contact customers and investors. A ransomware-as-a-service model lets affiliates rent malware and share proceeds, and cryptocurrency makes payments harder to trace. The speaker describes these groups as organized, well-funded operations that reinvest their earnings.

The middle section walks through a typical intrusion. It usually starts with phishing or a malicious link, followed by credential theft, lateral movement toward domain controllers, and data theft before encryption. Dwell times can stretch for months, and attackers may tamper with backups. Malware has also shifted from files on disk toward fileless, memory-resident techniques. The speaker compares modern ransomware gangs to historical pirates and privateers, arguing that cutting off safe havens, payment flows and recruitment may matter as much as technical controls. Backups and cyber insurance are discussed as helpful but imperfect recovery options, since paying a ransom does not guarantee full restoration.

The closing part argues for layered prevention that combines endpoint protection, behavior-based detection, and decoy canary files, with an emphasis on reducing alert fatigue for analysts. The speaker suggests insurers may begin requiring stronger defenses as a condition of coverage. For practitioners, the main takeaway is that stopping an intrusion early in the attack chain raises the cost for attackers, and that no single control is enough on its own.

talks.title: Three Worlds of Application / Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Maps application and cloud security across developer pipelines, cloud-native workloads, and governance, risk and compliance.
talks.summary:
The talk frames application and cloud security as one connected problem, since a cloud environment is itself built from applications. It starts with developer work and the CI/CD pipeline, arguing that a secure development lifecycle is about planning, design and analysis rather than only test environments. Secure coding areas such as authentication, authorization, validation, system management and cryptography are covered, along with how vulnerabilities are rated by severity and why teams need a clear policy for the risk they will accept.

Testing comes next, including software composition analysis, static, dynamic and interactive testing, with the argument that checks should be layered across each DevSecOps phase so a failed result stops a release from advancing. For production, the focus moves to native and on-premises controls such as web application firewalls, network and application security groups, attribute-based access control, key vaults, service mesh for microservices and container security tools. A recurring theme is weighing the intent of attackers, employees and contractors, and watching application behavior for patterns that look wrong.

The closing section treats governance, risk and compliance as the instruction manual, pointing to existing frameworks such as ISO 27001 and NIST rather than inventing controls from scratch. The takeaways are that security is everyone's responsibility, that authentication keeps evolving beyond passwords, and that organizations should budget resources for recovering from attacks.

talks.title: Why Should I Care? Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification DoD/NonDoD
talks.teaser: Explains the CMMC maturity levels and domains, and how organizations can use the model to plan cyber risk controls.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) to an audience that is mostly new to compliance. The speaker explains that the standard draws on NIST SP 800-171 and other frameworks, and that it applies to defense contractors handling federal contract information and controlled unclassified information. The model is organized into domains, capabilities and practices, with assessors checking at the practice level, and it progresses from basic cyber hygiene to advanced levels.

The maturity levels are walked through in order. Level one covers performed practices, level two adds documentation, level three adds planning and resourcing, and levels four and five add measured review and standardized, organization-wide processes. Media protection serves as the worked example, showing controls on removable media, marking CUI, and encrypting data during transport. The speaker expects most defense suppliers to target level three, and notes that cloud and managed service providers matter too, since forensic capability, data residency and personnel access shape whether an environment qualifies.

The closing argument is that the model helps even organizations outside defense work, because it gives a staged roadmap for managing cyber risk. Practical advice includes fixing technical gaps such as firewalls and endpoint protection before perfecting paperwork. The session ended with questions about reassessment every three years and the plan of action that follows an assessment.

talks.title: Raising the Average - Finding and Managing Mentors
talks.teaser: Explains how career changers can find, approach and manage three kinds of mentors through virtual networking.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who moved into IT after a sales career, opens by noting that many people starting out lack a mentor and feel unsure how to find one. He builds the talk around the idea that the people you spend most time with shape your growth. He argues that career changers often treat their earlier jobs as a weakness, when those experiences can make them stronger candidates.

He describes three mentor types. Subject matter experts work in the role you want and can explain their day-to-day work; a conversation with a penetration tester helped him rule out one path and pick another. Attesters are closer contacts who will vouch for you, act as references and help with a job search. Accountability partners are peers or people slightly ahead who check in on goals. To find people, he suggests looking at recorded webinars, conference speakers and event organizers, and reaching out with a short message. Calls should run about half an hour to an hour, with a clear agenda, written questions and an action item.

He stresses the follow-up: thank the person, summarize takeaways, set a next date and keep the relationship active. He also covers ending a mentorship gracefully, naming the relationship out loud, and the fact that mentoring others benefits the mentor. The closing message is to be specific, show up on video when possible, and recognize that trust is the main barrier for entry-level candidates.
